newsitem.title: UK: European bourses close up on benign US data.
newsitem.headline: European bourses close up on benign US data.

text.p: European bourses ended the week in buoyant mood on Friday, rising on figures showing restrained inflation in the United States, the world's most powerful economy.
London, Frankfurt and Paris drew strength from the U.S. Labour department data saying moderate increases in food and energy prices helped to subdue the overall rate of wholesale inflation.

On the currency markets, the dollar shrugged off the figures and remained at the levels seen earlier in the day, up slightly. Sterling was the star performer, hitting the high spots against the mark and dollar but on other factors.

London, Europe biggest bourse, closed up nearly one percent on the the strength of the U.S. data which traders said confirmed a benign U.S. inflation scenario with the prospects of subdued interest rates.
"When the data came out, it was sell, sell, sell. Then as people worked out the figures were basically in line, it was buy, buy, buy. We were pulled up by futures," a dealer said.
The FTSE 100 share index, which edged up slightly in nervous trading earlier, ended up 33.4 at 4028.1 points after the U.S. figures drove the Wall Street up 0.5 percent.
Frankfurt and Paris also showed gains after most European bourses registered losses on Thursday.
The poor performance followed a record-breaking pace by European bourses earlier this week which largely mirrored the bull market on Wall Street, driven by rapid growth and low inflation.

European investors took their direction from Friday's U.S. data because the state of the American economy largely sets the pace for global markets and any downturn there would quickly be felt on this side of the Atlantic.

In Frankfurt, floor trading ended in modest gains before the American inflation figures were issued, but transaction on the computerised IBIS DAX index ended up 0.34 percent after their release. In Paris, French shares registered a healthy 0.5 percent gain on the day after on the U.S. figures. But turnover was slow as many traders had remained on the sidelines awaiting the data.
The dollar edged higher, taking the price figures in its stride, as well as data on retail sales which posted a surprisingly strong rise in September, largely because of a surge in new car sales.
Total retail sales increased by 0.7 percent but excluding the automobile business, September retail sales were up a more modest 0.4 percent, indicating that economic activity was slowing.
"It's making people feel a bit more confident that there isn't a near-term U.S. inflation threat and consequently the dollar's rising," said Stephen King at HSBC James Capel.
The undoubted centre of attention was sterling, which powered to 20-month highs as the market rode a wave of euphoria gripping the ruling Conservatives after an upbeat party conference.

The pound broke through 2.40 marks in early business and pushed on to 2.4130 by late afternoon, compared to Thursday's 2.3943. It also rose strongly against the dollar, to $1.5753 in late trading after Thursday's level of $1.5654.
CURRENCIES
The dollar was at 1.5315 marks and 111.67 yen compared with 1.5300 marks and 111.26 yen late in Europe on Thursday.
STOCK MARKETS
The Financial Times-Stock Exchange index of 100 leading British shares ended 33.4 points higher at 4,028.1.
In Paris, the CAC-40 share index finished up 11.49 at 2,147.12.
The 30-share DAX index in Frankfurt closed up 5.28 at 2,686.03.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold closed at $381.35 an ounce, down 60 cents from Thursday. Silver finished at $5.02 up a cent.
